d.title: Decide the role first, then convert - not the other way round
d.caption: **Reading a file and then asking what the columns are is backwards.** Decide each column's role, then convert to it deliberately, because the conversion is where the sentinels get caught: an empty string, NA, N/A and −999 all have to become missing *before* the cast, or they become a category called “-999” or silently coerce to zero. **`errors="coerce"` is the argument that makes this safe** — anything unparseable becomes NaT or NaN rather than raising or passing through — and then counting the new missing values tells you how dirty the column really was.

d.title: Nothing above 0.71, and one column is exactly the sum of the other two
d.caption: **A correlation matrix is every pair, one pair at a time — so a feature that is a combination of two others can hide in plain sight.** Here c is a + b almost exactly, and the highest pairwise correlation is 0.71: a “drop anything above 0.9” rule keeps all three, and any linear model with all three has unstable coefficients. **The variance inflation factor is the measure that sees it, because it regresses each feature on all the others rather than on one at a time.** The same blind spot explains Simpson's paradox: a trend that reverses inside every group is invisible pairwise.

d.title: Every accuracy test is a comparison with something outside the table
d.caption: **A value can pass every other check and still be wrong: an email that is well-formed, unique, present and recent can belong to somebody else.** Accuracy is agreement with reality, and reality is not in the data — so there is no self-contained test for it, only three ways of reaching outside. **The miss column is what makes reconciliation insufficient on its own:** errors that net to zero pass it perfectly, and so does a figure that is wrong in both the table and the reference because they share an upstream source.

d.title: Five hundred billion pairs, or a few million
d.caption: **Comparing every record with every other is quadratic: a million customers is 500 billion pairs, which is not a tuning problem but an impossibility.** Blocking makes it many small problems by only comparing records that share a cheap key — and the whole design sits in one constraint: **the block key must be shared by true duplicates, so a typo in the block key separates a pair for ever.** Hence a key built from the parts typos usually miss. Then a cluster of matches has to collapse into one record, and that survivorship rule decides what actually remains.

d.title: One of the three mechanisms is testable, and the distinction that matters is not
d.caption: **MCAR is testable: if missingness is unrelated to everything, the rows with and without the value should look the same on every other column — so a difference on any column rules it out.** What cannot be tested is the one that changes what you should do: MAR against MNAR turns on whether missingness depends on the value you do not have, and no amount of data answers that. **So the honest procedure is to test for MCAR, gather evidence, and then reason about the collection process** — which is domain knowledge, not statistics.

d.title: Four imputations, in order of what they condition on
d.caption: **Each method is a different answer to “conditioned on what?”, and the ordering is roughly cheapest to most faithful.** A column mean conditions on nothing, so it flattens variance and weakens every correlation the column had. **The group-conditional fill is usually the best value for effort** — one line, and it respects the structure that actually drives the missingness. KNN and the iterative imputer condition on the other columns properly, at the cost of fitting a model inside your preprocessing, which then has to go inside the pipeline so it never sees the test set.

d.title: Several guesses, several analyses, one pooled answer
d.caption: **Single imputation treats each guess as a fact, which is why it produces standard errors that are too small** — the uncertainty about the filled value simply disappears from the arithmetic. Multiple imputation keeps it: draw from the predictive distribution rather than taking its mean, do that m times, run the analysis on each, and pool. **The spread between the m answers becomes part of the reported uncertainty**, which is what makes the interval honest. Reach for it when the confidence interval is the deliverable; a point prediction from a tree model rarely needs it.

d.title: Far from which rest?
d.caption: **A transaction of 400 is unremarkable overall, normal for a large store, and a glaring anomaly for a small one** — so a detector that pools everything misses the real outlier and flags perfectly ordinary large-store rows instead. The fix is to apply the same rule within the group. **The two rows below it are the time-series versions of the same mistake:** a value has to be compared against the series' own level, which drifts, and against the same hour or weekday, which cycles. Pooling across a trend flags the end of the series; pooling across a season flags every Monday.

state: a spike against the recent level

d.title: Change the model instead of the data
d.caption: **A squared-error loss makes one extreme row quadratically important, which is the whole reason it dominates the fit** — so if the value is genuine, the alternative to editing the data is choosing a loss that limits any row's influence. Huber is quadratic near the centre and linear in the tail; quantile regression models a percentile and never squares anything; a tree splits on order alone, so the magnitude of an extreme value is irrelevant to it. **And influence is not outlyingness: a wildly wrong y at a typical x barely moves the line, while a moderate error at an extreme x can rotate it.**

state: when the median is the target
